analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2017 tax law's individual tax cuts — lower rates, bigger standard deduction and child credit — permanent.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one cosponsor and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2023, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 tax law cut individual income tax rates, doubled the standard deduction and the child tax credit, capped deductions for state and local taxes, and raised the estate tax exemption — but wrote most of those individual provisions to expire after 2025. This bill would strike every expiration date and make them permanent. It also makes permanent the 20% deduction for owners of pass-through businesses and the higher alternative minimum tax exemption. The bill never moved past its committee referral, so none of it took effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Nearly every household that files income taxes keeps the 2017 rate cuts, the roughly doubled standard deduction, and the $2,000-per-child tax credit beyond 2025. But the biggest dollar gains go to the top: very wealthy families get a permanently doubled estate tax exemption, owners of partnerships and S corporations keep a permanent 20% deduction on business income, and the highest earners keep the 37% top rate and a much higher alternative minimum tax exemption.

how_it_helps.text: Makes the reduced individual income tax brackets — including the 37% top rate — permanent instead of letting them revert to pre-2017 rates after 2025.
Permanently keeps the roughly doubled standard deduction and the $2,000 child tax credit (up to $1,400 of it refundable), which are the provisions that reach the most middle-income families.
Makes permanent the doubled estate and gift tax exemption (the base amount rises from $5 million to $10 million per person, indexed for inflation), which matters only to the largest estates.
Makes permanent the 20% deduction for qualified business income of pass-through entities such as partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships.
Makes permanent the higher alternative minimum tax exemption, including raising the income level at which the exemption phases out to $1 million for joint filers.
Makes permanent the $10,000 cap on deducting state and local taxes and the lower $750,000 cap on deductible mortgage interest.
Permanently extends tax-free treatment for student loans discharged on account of death or disability, and expanded ABLE savings accounts for people with disabilities.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury — and ultimately taxpayers — bears the cost, because these cuts are extended permanently with no offsetting revenue. Outside distributional estimates consistently find the largest dollar gains from the 2017 individual provisions go to the highest-income households, so the permanent version concentrates its benefits at the top while adding to projected deficits.

drawbacks.text: The 2017 law set its individual provisions to expire after 2025 specifically to limit their official ten-year cost; this bill removes those sunset dates with no pay-fors, so it would add hundreds of billions of dollars a year to projected federal deficits.

The provisions with the largest dollar value — the doubled estate exemption, the permanent 37% top rate, the pass-through deduction, and the $1 million AMT phaseout — flow mainly to very high-income households and business owners, not to typical wage earners.

The child tax credit it makes permanent is not fully refundable (capped at $1,400 per child) and requires a Social Security number for each child, so families with little or no tax liability — the lowest-income families — gain little from it.

It locks in provisions that raise taxes on some filers: the $10,000 cap on state and local tax deductions hurts itemizers in high-tax states, and the permanent repeal of personal exemptions and most miscellaneous itemized deductions removes write-offs some families and workers used before 2017.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Middle-income families would keep real, meaningful tax cuts that are scheduled to lapse, and that is a genuine benefit. But the bill is not designed neutrally: it attaches permanence to the most top-heavy provisions of the 2017 law — the estate tax doubling, the pass-through carve-out, and AMT relief aimed above $1 million of income — without paying for any of it, so the long-run bill is a large, regressive, deficit-financed tax extension rather than a balanced one.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it simply expired when that Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Ted Cruz introduced the bill on April 20, 2023, with Senator Mike Braun as its only cosponsor.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance that same day, and no further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — was ever recorded.
The bill's one-page purpose, per the Congressional Research Service, was to make permanent the individual provisions of the 2017 tax law that were scheduled to expire at the end of 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly with almost no support, the largest estates and pass-through owners did not get their tax breaks locked in beyond what the 2017 law already provided, and the federal budget avoided the deficit increase permanence would have added. In practice, the tax cuts' 2025 sunset remained in place to be renegotiated in a later bill.

for.name: Sen. Ted Cruz
for.role: U.S. Senator from Texas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2017 individual tax provisions permanent and referred it to the Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. Mike Braun
for.role: U.S. Senator from Indiana; sole cosponsor

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled it for a hearing, markup, or vote; no committee action appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support was two Senate Republicans — the sponsor and one cosponsor out of 49 Senate Republicans — and no vote was ever held, so no member of either party had to take a public position on the floor.

industries.industry: Owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, S corporations, sole proprietors)
industries.note: The bill makes the 20% deduction on pass-through business income permanent, a tax break unavailable to wage earners. Outside analyses find most of its value goes to higher-earning owners, and permanence is financed by deficits rather than offsets.

industries.industry: The wealthiest households and large estates
industries.note: A permanently doubled estate and gift tax exemption (indexed from $10 million per person) benefits only the largest estates, worth millions per couple. Nothing in the bill provides an offsetting public benefit for the lost revenue.

Families keep the $2,000 child tax credit and the doubled standard deduction permanently. The gains are real but capped — the refundable portion stops at $1,400 per child, so the lowest-income families benefit least.

industries.industry: Homeowners and itemizers in high-tax states
industries.note: Making the $10,000 state and local tax deduction cap permanent locks in a higher effective tax for itemizers in states with high property and income taxes.
